lines.text: Today your programs learn to do maths and make decisions, just like a shopkeeper with a calculator.
input() always gives text, so "5" plus "3" would make "53".
Wrap it in int() to get a real number: int(input("How many? ")).
Now you can do maths with it.
Use + to add, - to subtract, * to multiply and / to divide.
Use // for whole-number division and % for the remainder.
Python follows BODMAS, just like your maths class.
Python compares with < > <= >= and ==, which means “is equal to”.
Use != for “is not equal to”.
Every comparison is either True or False.
if runs code only when a comparison is True. elif checks another option, and else catches everything left.
The lines inside must be indented by four spaces.
Watch what happens when we add two answers from input.
Without int we get fifty-three, because text just sticks together. With int we get eight.
Three samosas at forty rupees each cost one hundred and twenty rupees.
Two friends share the bill, so double slash divides it into whole rupees.
Python checks the first condition, and sixty-seven is not one hundred or more.
Then elif checks fifty or more, which is True, so we see Half century.
Notice the colon at the end and the four spaces before each print.
Python cannot compare text with a number, so it shows a TypeError.
The fix is to wrap the input in int, so money becomes a real number.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
